standard_text: Solve real-world and other mathematical problems by graphing points with rational number coordinates on a coordinate plane. Include the use of coordinates and absolute value to find distances between points with the same first coordinate or the same second coordinate.

progression.narrative: This standard asks students to graph points with rational coordinates in all four quadrants and to use coordinates and absolute value to find distances between points that share a first or second coordinate. The on-grade work runs from plotting and quadrant identification to the core distance rule: points that share a coordinate sit on one grid line, and the distance is the absolute value of the difference of the coordinates that do not match, applied in map and route problems. Students who struggle here usually carry gaps from well below grade six, most often weak number-line reading and no habit of following a rule to produce numbers in order. Intervention should start with those foundations, rebuild the grade five skills of plotting in the first quadrant and generating ordered pairs from two rules, and only then return to four-quadrant work with signed coordinates.

steps.rationale: Plotting is the physical act the standard's graphing demand rests on. Quadrant I with whole numbers lets the right-then-up convention get automatic before negative signs complicate it.
The standard requires all four quadrants. Reading a plotted point and naming its quadrant forces the key insight: the SIGNS of the coordinates, not the picture, locate the point.

The standard's explicit distance demand: points sharing a first or second coordinate sit on one grid line, and absolute value of the difference of the unmatched coordinates gives the distance -- always positive.
The 'solve real-world problems' heart of the standard: several straight-line distances on a map get found one at a time, then combined the way the question asks, with any unit scale applied.
The standard run in reverse and the bridge forward: given a distance instead of a second point, produce every point that far away along a grid line -- two per axis, four in all.

skills.name: Locate numbers on a number line and count the distance between two marks

prerequisite_skill.description: Place a whole number on a marked number line and find how far apart two numbers are by counting the jumps between them.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: On a number line, how far is it from 4 to 11?

skills.i_do_script: A number line is a ruler for numbers: each tick is one step, and the numbers grow as I move right. To place 7, I start at 0 and count 7 ticks to the right. To find how far apart 4 and 11 are, I put my finger on 4 and jump one tick at a time until I land on 11, counting each jump: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. That is 7 jumps, so 4 and 11 are 7 apart. I count the jumps between the marks, not the marks themselves.

canonical_error.pattern: Counts the tick marks instead of the jumps between them, landing one too high
canonical_error.example: Asked how far it is from 4 to 11, the student touches 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 while counting and answers 8.
canonical_error.why: The student counts positions instead of moves. Distance measures the spaces traveled, and the starting mark is not a jump.

skills.item_template: A number line from 0 to 20 with whole-number ticks. Student places a number, names a marked point, or counts the distance between two whole numbers. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: How far is it from 4 to 11 on a number line?
How far is it from 6 to 15?
How far is it from 0 to 8?
Start at 3 and jump 5 to the right. Where do you land?
Start at 12 and jump 4 to the left. Where do you land?
How far is it from 9 to 16?
Two marks are at 5 and 5. How far apart are they?
Which is farther from 10: the mark at 6 or the mark at 13?
sample_items.answer: The mark at 6 (4 away; 13 is only 3 away)

sample_items.stem: How far is it from 7 to 18?

redirect_script.stop: Are you counting marks or jumps?
redirect_script.prompt: Put your finger on the first number and count only the moves. Say a number each time your finger lands on a new tick, not when it starts.
redirect_script.praise: You counted the jumps, and that is exactly what distance measures.

vocabulary.definition: A line marked with equally spaced ticks, where each tick names a number and numbers grow to the right.
How many jumps it takes to get from one number to another. Distance is never negative.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 3 number line work: build a line with equal jumps from 0 and practice naming the tick your finger lands on.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a number line from 0 to 15. Circle 4 and circle 11.
How could we find out how far apart the circles are without a ruler?
Start at 4 and hop one tick at a time: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 hops lands on 11. So 4 and 11 are 7 apart. We count hops, not ticks.
If a student answers 8, they counted the starting mark. Have them hop with a pencil and say a number only when the pencil lands.
Your turn: how far is it from 6 to 15?

skills.name: Extend a number pattern that follows a rule

prerequisite_skill.description: Continue a whole-number pattern that follows an add or subtract rule, and name the rule from the terms.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: What are the next two numbers in 3, 7, 11, 15, ...?

skills.i_do_script: A pattern is a list of numbers built by one rule that repeats. To find the rule, I check what happens between neighbors. Watch: in 3, 7, 11, 15, each number is 4 more than the one before, because 7 - 3 = 4 and 11 - 7 = 4. So the rule is add 4. To extend, I keep applying it: 15 + 4 = 19, then 19 + 4 = 23. On a number line the pattern is equal jumps of 4, so the terms are equally spaced.

canonical_error.pattern: Checks only the first pair of terms, or adds the wrong constant, then extends with a broken rule
canonical_error.example: For 3, 7, 11, 15, the student sees 3 and 7, decides the rule is add 3 because the list starts at 3, and writes 18 next.
canonical_error.why: The student guesses the rule from one clue instead of testing it between every pair of neighbors. A rule only counts if it works for the whole list.

skills.item_template: A four-term whole-number pattern with an add or subtract rule (step 2 to 9). Student names the rule or writes the next one or two terms. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: What is the rule for 3, 7, 11, 15?
sample_items.answer: Add 4

sample_items.stem: What are the next two numbers in 3, 7, 11, 15, ...?
What is the next number in 5, 10, 15, 20, ...?
What is the rule for 40, 34, 28, 22?
sample_items.answer: Subtract 6

sample_items.stem: What is the next number in 40, 34, 28, 22, ...?
Start at 2 and use the rule add 3. Write the first four numbers.
What are the next two numbers in 1, 8, 15, 22, ...?
Start at 50 and use the rule subtract 9. Write the first three numbers.
What is the missing number in 6, 13, __, 27?

redirect_script.stop: Does your rule work between every pair of neighbors?
redirect_script.prompt: Subtract each number from the next one, all the way down the list. The rule is the jump that shows up every single time.
redirect_script.praise: You tested the rule on the whole list, so you know it is really the rule.

vocabulary.definition: A list of numbers built by repeating one rule.
The instruction that gets you from one number in a pattern to the next, like add 4.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 4 skip counting on a number line: make equal jumps from a start number and record where you land.

worked_example_script.text: Write 3, 7, 11, 15 on the board with an empty arc drawn between each pair of neighbors.
What jump takes 3 to 7? Does the same jump take 7 to 11? And 11 to 15?
Every arc is a jump of 4, so the rule is add 4. Keep jumping: 15 + 4 = 19 and 19 + 4 = 23. On a number line the terms sit 4 apart, in a straight march.
If a student writes 18 next, ask them to test their rule on the arc from 7 to 11. Add 3 fails there, so it is not the rule.
Your turn: find the rule for 40, 34, 28, 22 and write the next number.

skills.name: Plot and name points in the first quadrant of the coordinate plane

prerequisite_skill.description: Plot a point with whole-number coordinates in the first quadrant, and read the coordinates of a plotted point, using the over-then-up convention.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: To plot (3, 5), how far do you go over, and how far up?

skills.i_do_script: An ordered pair is a set of directions from the origin, and the order never changes: over first, then up. Watch: to plot (3, 5), I start at (0, 0), move 3 to the right along the x-axis, then 5 up. I mark the point where those two moves meet. To read a plotted point, I run the trip backwards: drop straight down to the x-axis and read that number first, then look across to the y-axis for the second number. (3, 5) and (5, 3) are different points because the trips are different.

canonical_error.pattern: Reverses the ordered pair, going up first and over second
canonical_error.example: Asked to plot (3, 5), the student goes up 3 and over 5, landing at (5, 3).
canonical_error.why: The student treats the pair as two loose numbers instead of an ordered trip. The first number always belongs to the x-axis, the horizontal move, no matter which number is bigger.

skills.item_template: A first-quadrant grid from 0 to 10 with whole-number coordinates. Student plots a named point, reads a plotted point, or names a point on an axis. Numeric or short response.

sample_items.stem: To plot (3, 5), which move comes first?
sample_items.answer: Over 3 to the right

sample_items.stem: Plot the point (4, 2). How far over and how far up do you go?
sample_items.answer: Over 4, up 2

sample_items.stem: A point sits 6 to the right of the origin and 1 up. What are its coordinates?
A point is plotted at over 2, up 7. Which ordered pair names it?
sample_items.distractor_logic: (7, 2) is the reversed pair; (2, 2) and (7, 7) repeat one coordinate for students who lose track of one move.

sample_items.stem: What are the coordinates of the origin?
The point (5, 0) sits on which axis?
sample_items.answer: The x-axis

sample_items.stem: The point (0, 4) sits on which axis?
sample_items.answer: The y-axis

sample_items.stem: Is (2, 6) the same point as (6, 2)? Explain.
sample_items.answer: No. (2, 6) is over 2 and up 6; (6, 2) is over 6 and up 2. The trips end in different places.

redirect_script.stop: Which move comes first, over or up?
redirect_script.prompt: Say the trip out loud before you move: over, then up. Underline the first number and label it x, then underline the second and label it y.
redirect_script.praise: Over then up, every time. That is the convention.

vocabulary.definition: Two numbers in parentheses (x, y) that give directions to one point: over x, then up y.
The point (0, 0) where the x-axis and y-axis cross. Every trip starts there.
The horizontal number line on the coordinate plane.
The vertical number line on the coordinate plane.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a first-quadrant grid from 0 to 8. Write (3, 5) on the board without plotting it.
The trip starts at the origin. Which number is the over move, and which is the up move?
Over 3 along the x-axis, then up 5. Mark the point where the two moves meet. The first number always rides the horizontal axis.
If a student goes up 3 first, have them trace the trip with a finger while saying over 3, up 5 out loud, then compare where the two trips end.
Your turn: plot (5, 3) on the same grid. Is it the same point as (3, 5)?

practice_problems.stem: On a number line, start at 0 and move over 4. Now imagine moving up 2 from there. What ordered pair did you just walk?
In the ordered pair (6, 3), which number is the x-coordinate?
Plot the point (2, 7). Describe the trip from the origin.
practice_problems.answer: Over 2 to the right, then up 7.

practice_problems.stem: A point is plotted over 5 and up 5. What are its coordinates, and what is special about it?
practice_problems.answer: (5, 5). Its coordinates are equal, so reversing them names the same point.

practice_problems.stem: Point A sits on the x-axis, 8 units from the origin. What are its coordinates?
Ella plotted a playground at (1, 6) and a fountain at (6, 1). Are they at the same spot? How do you know?
practice_problems.answer: No. The playground is over 1 and up 6; the fountain is over 6 and up 1. The order of the numbers changes the trip.

practice_problems.stem: Name a point that sits on the y-axis and is 3 units from the origin.
Marcus plotted (3, 5) by going up 3 and over 5. Find his mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Marked the point at over 5, up 3.
practice_problems.answer: He reversed the order. The first number is the over move: go over 3, then up 5. He actually plotted (5, 3).

activities.title: Walk the Grid
materials: Tape grid on the floor, 0 to 6 on each axis
activities.instructions:
1. A student draws a card, like (4, 2), and stands on the origin.
2. They walk the trip while the group chants it: over 4, up 2. Drop a beanbag where they stop.
3. The group checks by reading the point backwards: drop to the x-axis, read 4; look across, read 2.
4. Repeat with a reversed card like (2, 4) and compare the two beanbag spots.
5. Say each time: over first, then up.

activities.title: First-Quadrant Treasure Hunt
materials: Two first-quadrant grids per pair (0 to 8)
activities.instructions:
1. Each partner hides three treasures at grid points and keeps the map hidden.
2. Partners take turns calling ordered pairs; the opponent answers hit or miss.
3. Every call must be spoken as a trip: over 3, up 6, before the guess counts.
4. First to find all three treasures wins.
5. Debrief question: why did calling (3, 6) never find a treasure hidden at (6, 3)?

strategy_links.why: Walking the trip on a floor grid makes the over-then-up convention physical before it becomes a rule.
The reversed-pair error is stable and predictable; fixing Marcus's plot confronts it head on.
Rapid over-then-up call and response builds the automatic first-number-is-x recall plotting runs on.

questioning_prompts: Which number in the pair is the over move? How do you know?
Where does every plotting trip start?
How would you read the coordinates of a point someone else plotted?
Is (2, 6) the same point as (6, 2)? Prove it with two trips.
A point sits on the x-axis. What must its y-coordinate be?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student goes up first and lands at the reversed point.
misconception_redirects.say: Trace both trips with your finger: over 3 up 5, then over 5 up 3. They end in different places, so the order matters. First number goes over.
misconception_redirects.praise: You went over first, then up. The trip matches the pair now.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student reads a plotted point by guessing which axis to check first.
misconception_redirects.say: Drop straight down from the point to the x-axis and read that number first. Then look straight across to the y-axis.
misconception_redirects.praise: Down for x, across for y. You read it in the right order.

quick_checks.look_for: Over 1 then up 4. Landing at over 4, up 1 means the pair got reversed.

quick_checks.prompt: What are the coordinates of a point on the y-axis, 7 up from the origin?
quick_checks.look_for: (0, 7), with the zero in the x spot.

worked_solution.stem: Plot the point (3, 5) on a first-quadrant grid.
worked_solution.answer: The point sits over 3 and up 5 from the origin.

steps.annotation: Every plotting trip starts where the axes cross.

steps.math: First number 3: move 3 right along the x-axis
steps.annotation: The first number is always the horizontal move.
The second number is always the vertical move.

steps.math: Mark the point where the moves meet
steps.annotation: Check by reading it backwards: down to the x-axis gives 3, across gives 5.

faded_example.stem: Plot the point (6, 2) on a first-quadrant grid.
faded_example.answer: The point sits over 6 and up 2 from the origin.

steps.annotation: The trip always starts at the origin.

steps.math: First number 6: move 6 right along the x-axis
steps.annotation: The over move comes first.
Make the up move. How far?
Mark the point and check it by reading it backwards.

sentence_starters: To plot (___, ___), I go over ___ and then up ___.
The first number is the x-coordinate, so it tells me to move ___.

skills.name: Generate two number patterns from rules and graph the ordered pairs

prerequisite_skill.description: Use two given rules to build two number patterns from the same starting number, pair the corresponding terms as ordered pairs, and plot them in the first quadrant.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Pattern A starts at 0 and adds 1. Pattern B starts at 0 and adds 3. What are the first three ordered pairs (A, B)?

skills.i_do_script: Two rules can build two patterns side by side, and matching terms become ordered pairs. Watch: Pattern A starts at 0 and adds 1, so A is 0, 1, 2, 3. Pattern B starts at 0 and adds 3, so B is 0, 3, 6, 9. I pair the terms that were born together: (0, 0), (1, 3), (2, 6), (3, 9). Then I plot each pair, over A and up B. The points march in a straight line because every step goes over 1 and up 3, the same jump every time.

canonical_error.pattern: Pairs terms from different positions, or plots the pair with the axes swapped
canonical_error.example: For A: 0, 1, 2, 3 and B: 0, 3, 6, 9, the student pairs 1 with 6 because both are 'second-ish', or plots (1, 3) by going over 3 and up 1.
canonical_error.why: The student loses track of which terms correspond. Each ordered pair must take its two numbers from the same position in the two lists, A first, B second.

skills.item_template: Two add-rule patterns from given starts (whole numbers, terms under 30). Student extends both patterns, writes the ordered pairs of corresponding terms, or plots them on a first-quadrant grid.

sample_items.stem: Pattern A: start at 0, add 2. Write the first four terms.
Pattern B: start at 0, add 5. Write the first four terms.
Using A: 0, 2, 4, 6 and B: 0, 5, 10, 15, write the four ordered pairs (A, B).
Pattern A starts at 1 and adds 1. Pattern B starts at 2 and adds 2. What is the third ordered pair (A, B)?
A: 0, 1, 2, 3 and B: 0, 4, 8, 12. Which ordered pair belongs to this table?
sample_items.distractor_logic: (8, 2) swaps the axes; (1, 8) and (2, 4) pair terms from different positions in the two lists.

sample_items.stem: The pairs (0, 0), (1, 3), (2, 6) follow two add rules. What is the next pair?
In the pair (2, 6) from patterns A and B, which pattern does the 6 come from?
sample_items.answer: Pattern B, the second number

sample_items.stem: A: start at 0, add 1. B: start at 0, add 1. Describe the points you would plot.
sample_items.answer: (0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 2), and so on. Each point goes over and up the same amount.

redirect_script.stop: Do both numbers in your pair come from the same position?
redirect_script.prompt: Line the two patterns up in a table, A on top and B below. Each column is one ordered pair: A over, B up.
redirect_script.praise: You paired the terms born together and plotted A over, B up. That is the whole skill.

vocabulary.definition: Terms that sit in the same position in two patterns, like the third term of each. They pair up to make one ordered pair.
The instruction that builds a pattern from its start, like add 3.

worked_example_script.text: Make a two-row table. Row A: start at 0, add 1, so 0, 1, 2, 3. Row B: start at 0, add 3, so 0, 3, 6, 9.
Which term of B was born at the same step as the 2 in A?
Each column of the table is one ordered pair: (0, 0), (1, 3), (2, 6), (3, 9). Plot each one, over A and up B. The points line up because every step is over 1 and up 3.
If a student pairs 1 with 6, point at the table columns: the 1 and the 3 share a column, so they pair. Columns, not guesses.
Your turn: A starts at 0 and adds 2, B starts at 0 and adds 4. Write and plot the first three pairs.

practice_problems.stem: Pattern A: start at 0, add 1. Write the first four terms.
Pattern B: start at 0, add 4. Write the first four terms.
Using A: 0, 1, 2, 3 and B: 0, 4, 8, 12, write the four ordered pairs (A, B).
Plot the pairs (0, 0), (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6) on a first-quadrant grid. What do you notice about the points?
practice_problems.answer: They lie on a straight line; each point is over 1 and up 2 from the last.

practice_problems.stem: Pattern A starts at 2 and adds 2. Pattern B starts at 3 and adds 3. What is the fourth ordered pair (A, B)?
The pairs (0, 0), (2, 3), (4, 6), (6, 9) come from two add rules starting at 0. What are the rules?
practice_problems.answer: A: add 2. B: add 3.

practice_problems.stem: A adds 1 and B adds 5, both starting at 0. Without listing the patterns, what is the sixth ordered pair (A, B)?
practice_problems.answer: (5, 25). After five steps, A is 5 and B is 25.

practice_problems.stem: Nia built A: 0, 1, 2, 3 and B: 0, 3, 6, 9, then wrote the pairs (0, 0), (1, 6), (2, 9). Find her mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: She paired terms from different positions. Corresponding terms share a position: (0, 0), (1, 3), (2, 6), (3, 9).

activities.title: Two Machines, One Table
materials: Two paper 'rule machines' (folded cards labeled with a rule)
activities.instructions:
1. Machine A gets the rule add 1; Machine B gets add 3. Both start at 0.
2. Partners take turns cranking a machine: say the rule, add counters, record the new term in a two-row table.
3. After four cranks each, circle each column of the table and write it as an ordered pair.
4. Plot every pair, over A and up B, and connect the dots with a straightedge.
5. Debrief question: why did equal cranks make the points march in a straight line?

activities.title: Pair the Pairs
materials: Rule cards and ordered-pair strips (cut apart)
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the rule cards, like A: add 2 and B: add 6, start 0, next to ordered-pair strips.
2. Match each pair of rules to the strip that lists its first four ordered pairs.
3. To claim a match, say how you checked one pair in the middle of the strip, not just the first.
4. Two decoy strips pair terms from different positions; set them aside and explain the mix-up.

pairs.left: A: add 1, B: add 3, both start 0
A: add 2, B: add 6, both start 0
A: add 1, B: add 4, both start 0
A: add 3, B: add 3, both start 0

strategy_links.why: Cranking two rule machines and tabling the outputs makes corresponding terms concrete before pairs are plotted.
Thinking aloud while pairing, this column gives the A and the B, makes the invisible matching step audible.
Fixing Nia's mispaired table targets the exact position-tracking error this skill produces.

questioning_prompts: Which two terms were born at the same step? How does the table show that?
In the pair (2, 6), which pattern does each number come from?
What move takes each plotted point to the next one?
Why do the points lie on a straight line?
If both rules doubled, what would happen to the picture?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student pairs terms from different positions in the two lists.
misconception_redirects.say: Stack the patterns in a two-row table and draw a box around each column. A pair is one box: A on top, B underneath.
misconception_redirects.praise: You took both numbers from one column, so the pair is true to the patterns.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student plots (1, 3) by going over 3 and up 1.
misconception_redirects.say: A is the first number, so A goes over. Say the trip before you move: over 1, up 3.
misconception_redirects.praise: Over A, up B. The graph matches the table now.

quick_checks.prompt: A: 0, 2, 4 and B: 0, 7, 14. What is the second ordered pair?
quick_checks.look_for: (2, 7). An answer of (2, 14) or (4, 7) means positions are slipping.

worked_solution.stem: Pattern A starts at 0 and adds 1. Pattern B starts at 0 and adds 3. Write and plot the first four ordered pairs (A, B).
worked_solution.answer: (0, 0), (1, 3), (2, 6), (3, 9), plotted over A and up B, lying on a straight line.

steps.annotation: Apply add 1 three times from the start.
Apply add 3 three times from the start.
Pair corresponding terms: same position, A first.

steps.math: Plot each pair: over A, up B
steps.annotation: Every step goes over 1 and up 3, so the points line up.

faded_example.stem: Pattern A starts at 0 and adds 2. Pattern B starts at 0 and adds 4. Write and plot the first four ordered pairs (A, B).

steps.annotation: Add 2 three times from the start.
Add 4 three times from the start.
Pair the corresponding terms, A first.
Plot the pairs, over A and up B. What shape do they make?

sentence_starters: The terms ___ and ___ correspond because they are both in position ___.
I plotted (___, ___) by going over ___ and up ___.

skills.name: Identify the quadrant of a point and read coordinates from a grid

prerequisite_skill.description: Know which axis is x and which is y, and that the four quadrants are numbered I, II, III, IV starting from the top-right and moving counterclockwise.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: If a point has a negative x and a positive y, which quadrant is it in?

skills.i_do_script: The quadrant numbers aren't sprinkled at random -- they ride one counterclockwise sweep that launches from the all-positive corner, so find that corner first and let your finger count the rest. The coordinate plane has four quadrants. Quadrant I is top-right (both x and y are positive). Quadrant II is top-left (x is negative, y is positive). Quadrant III is bottom-left (both negative). Quadrant IV is bottom-right (x is positive, y is negative). I count the quadrants like a backwards C, starting at the top-right. Watch: for the point (-4, 3), x is negative and y is positive, so this is Quadrant II.

canonical_error.pattern: Numbers the quadrants clockwise starting from top-right (I, IV, III, II) instead of counterclockwise (I, II, III, IV).
canonical_error.example: Asked to name the quadrant of (-4, 3), the student says Quadrant IV because they think 'top-left = the second one I count going clockwise.'
canonical_error.why: The convention is counterclockwise but most students read English text top-to-bottom and left-to-right, so they default to clockwise numbering until corrected.

redirect_script.stop: Pause — which way do we count quadrants?
redirect_script.prompt: Start at the top-right (where both signs are positive) and trace counterclockwise: I, II, III, IV. Now find your point.
redirect_script.praise: Right — top-right is one, then go counterclockwise. Locked in.

vocabulary.definition: One of the four sections the x-axis and y-axis divide the coordinate plane into.
The pair of numbers (x, y) that name a point's location.
To mark a point on the coordinate plane at a given ordered pair.

practice_problems.stem: In which quadrant are both the x- and y-coordinates positive?
practice_problems.answer: Quadrant I

practice_problems.stem: What are the signs of the coordinates of every point in Quadrant III?
practice_problems.answer: Both negative -- the point looks like (-x, -y).

practice_problems.stem: In which quadrant is the point (-4, 3)?
practice_problems.answer: Quadrant II
practice_problems.notes: The classic clockwise-counter says Quadrant IV here -- listen for how they count.

practice_problems.stem: In which quadrant is the point (5, -2)?
practice_problems.answer: Quadrant IV

practice_problems.stem: A student named the quadrant of (-6, 2). Find the mistake and fix it.
shown_work: x is negative and y is positive, so the point is top-left.
Top-right is I. Counting clockwise: top-left must be the fourth one.
practice_problems.answer: The location was right -- top-left -- but quadrants count COUNTERCLOCKWISE from the top-right: I, II, III, IV. Top-left is Quadrant II.
practice_problems.notes: Baits the canonical clockwise-numbering error.

practice_problems.stem: What are the coordinates of point A, and which quadrant is it in?
practice_problems.answer: A is at (-2, -5), in Quadrant III.
practice_problems.notes: Watch for the pair read backwards as (-5, -2).

practice_problems.stem: A point has a negative y-coordinate and sits exactly on the y-axis. What is its x-coordinate, and is it inside any quadrant?
practice_problems.answer: Its x-coordinate is 0, and it is not in any quadrant -- points on an axis belong to no quadrant.

practice_problems.stem: Give the coordinates of any point in Quadrant II that is 4 units from the y-axis.
practice_problems.answer: Any point (-4, y) with y positive, such as (-4, 5).
practice_problems.notes: Producing a point reverses the skill -- signs must be chosen, not just read.

activities.title: Sign Pattern Sort
activities.instructions:
1. Lay out the five headers: Quadrant I, II, III, IV, and On an axis.
2. Partners take turns drawing a card, saying the signs out loud ('negative, negative'), and placing it.
3. The partner agrees or challenges before the next draw -- a challenge means both explain.
4. Debrief question: how can you name the quadrant without ever seeing a grid?

activities.title: Why Did Maya Say Quadrant IV?
materials: One printed problem card per group
activities.instructions:
1. Show Maya's work and let the group talk before you do.
2. Ask: what was Maya thinking? (Her reasoning is sensible -- we read pages clockwise-ish, top to bottom.)
3. Have the group trace a backwards C on a sketched plane, counting I, II, III, IV out loud.
4. Each student writes Maya a one-sentence tip.

content.worked_problem: Name the quadrant of (-4, 3). Maya's answer: Quadrant IV, because 'top-left is the fourth corner I read.'
content.error_step: Maya numbered the quadrants clockwise, the way she reads a page.
content.why: Quadrants count counterclockwise starting at the top-right: I (top-right), II (top-left), III (bottom-left), IV (bottom-right). Top-left is Quadrant II.

activities.title: Four Corners Quadrants
materials: Four corner signs: Quadrant I, II, III, IV (hung counterclockwise)
activities.instructions:
1. Hang the quadrant signs so the room matches a coordinate plane: I front-right, II front-left, III back-left, IV back-right.
2. Call an ordered pair, like (-3, 7). On 'move,' every student walks to the matching corner.
3. Ask one student in the majority corner to justify with signs: 'negative x means left, positive y means up.'
4. Sneak in axis points like (0, 5) -- the correct move is to stand in the middle aisle, not a corner.
5. Debrief question: which sign pattern goes with each corner?

strategy_links.why: Rapid choral 'signs to quadrant' calls build the automatic sign-pattern recall this skill runs on.
Analyzing a clockwise-counted answer surfaces the quadrant-numbering misconception directly.
Whiteboard Pass makes every student's quadrant call visible on each ordered pair.

questioning_prompts: Before you look at the grid -- what do the SIGNS of the coordinates tell you?
Which quadrant is number one, and which way do we count from there?
Negative x moves you which way? Positive y moves you which way?
The point (0, -6) -- is it in a quadrant at all? Why or why not?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student numbers the quadrants clockwise from top-right and calls a top-left point Quadrant IV.
misconception_redirects.say: Start at the top-right (where both signs are positive) and trace counterclockwise: I, II, III, IV. Now find your point.
misconception_redirects.praise: Right -- top-right is one, then go counterclockwise. Locked in.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student reads a plotted point backwards -- writes (3, -5) for a point at (-5, 3).
misconception_redirects.say: From the point, slide your finger straight DOWN or UP to the x-axis and read that number first. Then slide straight across to the y-axis for the second number.
misconception_redirects.praise: You read x from the x-axis first -- that's exactly how coordinates come off a grid.

quick_checks.prompt: Tell me the sign pattern for Quadrant III.
quick_checks.look_for: 'Both negative,' fast. Hesitation or 'negative, positive' means the sign-to-quadrant map isn't set.
Quadrant III instantly. 'Quadrant II' often signals clockwise counting; a long pause means they need the grid every time.

worked_example_script.text: Sketch the plane and mark the corner where BOTH coordinates come out positive -- top-right. That all-positive corner is the starting block, Quadrant I. Now sweep counterclockwise -- the same turn that lifts the positive x-axis up toward the positive y-axis -- stamping II, III, IV as you go.

Sweep with your finger from the starting block and count: one... two. Where is your finger when you say 'two'? Top-left -- the region where x is negative and y is positive. Which of those signs match the point (-4, 3)?
Sketch a coordinate plane with the four quadrants and write the point (-4, 3) on the board -- but do not plot it yet.
The x-coordinate is -4. Does that put the point left or right of the y-axis?
The y-coordinate is 3. Is the point above or below the x-axis?
Left and up -- so the point lives in the top-left region. Now we just need that region's number.
Where does Quadrant I live, and which way do we count from there -- clockwise or counterclockwise?
If the student counts clockwise and says Quadrant IV, have them trace a backwards C starting at the top-right, saying 'I, II, III, IV' out loud.
So which quadrant is (-4, 3) in? And what sign pattern does every point in that quadrant share?
Negative x, positive y -- top-left -- Quadrant II. The signs alone tell you the quadrant before you ever plot the point.

worked_solution.stem: In which quadrant is the point (-4, 3)?

steps.math: x = -4 -> negative -> LEFT of the y-axis
steps.annotation: The sign of the x-coordinate says which side of the y-axis you're on.
The sign of the y-coordinate says above or below the x-axis.
You can locate the region from the signs alone -- no plotting needed.

steps.math: Count counterclockwise from top-right: I, II -> Quadrant II
steps.annotation: Quadrant I is top-right; the count goes counterclockwise, like a backwards C.

faded_example.stem: In which quadrant is the point (5, -6)?

steps.math: x = 5 -> positive -> RIGHT of the y-axis
steps.annotation: The x-sign is worked out for you.
Is y = -6 above or below the x-axis? Write the direction.
Right and down is which quadrant? Count counterclockwise from top-right.

sentence_starters: The x-coordinate is ___, so the point is to the ___ of the y-axis.
I knew it was Quadrant ___ because the signs are ___ and ___.

skills.name: Find the distance between two points that share an x- or y-coordinate

prerequisite_skill.description: Recognize that two points with the same x lie on a vertical line and two points with the same y lie on a horizontal line, and that the distance is the absolute value of the difference of the unmatched coordinates.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Points (2, -3) and (2, 5) share an x. What is the distance between them?

skills.i_do_script: When two points share an x-coordinate, they sit on the same vertical line — the only thing that changes is y, so I subtract the y-values and take the absolute value. Same idea when they share a y-coordinate: only x changes, so I subtract the x-values and take the absolute value. Watch: for A(-14, 8) and B(6, 8), the y-values match, so distance = |6 - (-14)| = |20| = 20 units. The absolute value bars guarantee the distance is positive.

canonical_error.pattern: Subtracts the two coordinates without using absolute value, then reports a negative distance, OR subtracts the wrong pair of coordinates (the matching ones) and gets zero.
canonical_error.example: Asked the distance between (-14, 8) and (6, 8), the student writes -14 - 6 = -20 and circles -20 as the answer; or they subtract 8 - 8 = 0 because those are the numbers that 'look different in position.'
canonical_error.why: The student has not connected 'distance' to 'always positive' — they treat distance as ordinary subtraction. Or they have not noticed that the matching coordinate is the one that does NOT change, so the subtraction must happen on the OTHER coordinate.

redirect_script.stop: Hold up — distance can't be negative.
redirect_script.prompt: Circle the coordinate that is the SAME in both points. Now subtract the OTHER coordinate, and put absolute-value bars around your answer.
redirect_script.praise: Yes — the matching coordinate stays put, the other one tells the distance.

vocabulary.definition: How far a number is from zero. Distance is always written with absolute value bars so it stays positive.
One of the two numbers in an ordered pair — the x-coordinate or the y-coordinate.

practice_problems.stem: On a number line, how far apart are -3 and 5?
practice_problems.answer: 8 units

practice_problems.stem: The points (2, 1) and (2, 6) share which coordinate, and do they line up vertically or horizontally?
practice_problems.answer: They share the x-coordinate, 2 -- so they line up vertically.

practice_problems.stem: What is the distance between the points (-14, 8) and (6, 8)?
practice_problems.answer: 20 units
practice_problems.notes: Crossing the y-axis: |6 - (-14)| = 20. Watch for 8 - 8 = 0 or -20.

practice_problems.stem: What is the distance between the points (4, -3) and (4, 9)?
practice_problems.answer: 12 units

practice_problems.stem: A student found the distance between (-9, 5) and (3, 5). Find the mistake and fix it.
shown_work: The y-values match, so subtract the x-values.
practice_problems.answer: The setup was right, but distance can never be negative. Put the subtraction inside absolute value bars: |3 - (-9)| = |12| = 12 units.
practice_problems.notes: Baits the canonical negative-distance error.

practice_problems.stem: Which expression gives the distance between (-4, 2) and (6, 2)?
practice_problems.notes: Points on opposite sides of the y-axis: 4 to the axis plus 6 past it = 10. Matches the item spec's expression format.

practice_problems.stem: Point A is at (7, -2). Point B is 9 units directly below A. What are B's coordinates?
practice_problems.notes: Reverses the skill: distance is given, a coordinate is missing. -2 - 9 = -11.

practice_problems.stem: Two points are 5 units apart and both have a y-coordinate of 3. One point is (-1, 3). Name BOTH points the other one could be.
practice_problems.notes: -1 + 5 = 4 and -1 - 5 = -6. Finding only one previews the 6AF5-S4 misconception.

activities.title: Walk the Distance
materials: Tape number line on the floor from -10 to 10 (or a large printed one)
activities.instructions:
1. Drop the beanbags on two numbers, like -3 and 4.
2. A student stands on one beanbag and walks to the other, counting every step out loud -- including the steps on the negative side.
3. The group writes the matching absolute value expression, like |4 - (-3)| = 7, and checks it against the step count.
4. Repeat with both numbers negative.
5. Debrief question: why does the expression give the same number as your feet did?

activities.title: Match the Points to the Distance
materials: Point-pair cards and expression cards (cut apart)
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the point-pair cards face up on the left and the expression cards on the right.
2. Partners take turns matching a pair of points to the absolute value expression that gives their distance.
3. Before locking a match, the chooser must say which coordinate matches and which one gets subtracted.
4. Two decoy expressions match nothing -- explain why they're wrong.
5. Debrief question: how do you decide WHICH coordinates to subtract?

activities.title: Line-Ship Battleship
materials: Two four-quadrant grids per pair (-8 to 8)
activities.instructions:
1. Each partner hides two 'ships': straight segments 3 to 5 units long drawn ALONG a grid line (horizontal or vertical), endpoints on grid points.
2. Partners take turns calling ordered pairs; the opponent answers hit or miss.
3. When a player has found both endpoints of a ship, they must state its length with an absolute value expression, like |5 - (-2)| = 7... if the length is wrong, the ship isn't sunk!
4. First to sink both ships wins.
5. Debrief question: why did every ship's length come from subtracting just ONE pair of coordinates?

strategy_links.why: Counting grid spaces (concrete) before writing |a - b| (abstract) shows why the absolute value rule works.
A worked distance example followed by a flawed negative-distance solution targets this skill's exact bug.
Short number talks on 'how far apart are -3 and 5' build the crossing-zero reasoning distances depend on.

questioning_prompts: Which coordinate is the SAME in both points? What does that tell you about the line they sit on?
Can a distance ever be negative? Why not?
Do these points sit on a vertical line or a horizontal line? How do you know without plotting?
Could you count the grid spaces to check your subtraction? Do it.
The points are on opposite sides of an axis -- how does the distance to the axis help you?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student reports a negative distance, or subtracts the matching coordinates and gets zero.
misconception_redirects.say: Circle the coordinate that is the SAME in both points. Now subtract the OTHER coordinate, and put absolute-value bars around your answer.
misconception_redirects.praise: Yes -- the matching coordinate stays put, the other one tells the distance.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student counts grid marks instead of spaces and comes out one unit too high (or low).
misconception_redirects.say: Count the SPACES between the two points, not the dots. Put your pencil in the first gap and count each jump.
misconception_redirects.praise: You counted the jumps -- that's what distance measures.

quick_checks.look_for: 8 units. An answer of -8 means no absolute value; 0 means they subtracted the matching x-coordinates instead.

quick_checks.prompt: Which pair sits on a horizontal line: (2, 5) and (2, 9), or (1, 4) and (7, 4)?
quick_checks.look_for: The second pair -- matching y means horizontal. Choosing the first pair means 'same x' and 'horizontal' are still fused.

worked_example_script.text: Write the two points on the board: A(-14, 8) and B(6, 8).
Look at the two ordered pairs. Which coordinate is the same in both points?
If the y-coordinates match, do these points line up vertically or horizontally? Picture the grid.
Only the x-values are different. What subtraction would tell us how far apart -14 and 6 are?
If the student writes -14 - 6 = -20 and stops, ask: 'Can two points be negative twenty apart?' Guide them to wrap the subtraction in absolute value bars: |6 - (-14)|.
Write: distance = |6 - (-14)| = |20| = 20 units.
Check it a second way: from -14 to 0 is how far? From 0 to 6? What do those two pieces add up to?
Find the matching coordinate, subtract the OTHER one, and take the absolute value. Distance is always positive.

worked_solution.stem: What is the distance between the points (-14, 8) and (6, 8)?

steps.annotation: The points sit on the same horizontal line -- only x changes.
Subtract the coordinates that are DIFFERENT, inside absolute value bars.
The bars keep distance positive, even when a coordinate is negative.
Check on the grid: -14 to 0 is 14 units, 0 to 6 is 6 more. 14 + 6 = 20.

faded_example.stem: What is the distance between the points (5, -7) and (5, 3)?

steps.math: x-coordinates match: 5 and 5 -> vertical line, only y changes.
steps.annotation: The matching coordinate is found for you.
Write the subtraction of the y-coordinates inside absolute value bars.
Compute it. Is your distance positive?

sentence_starters: The ___-coordinates match, so I subtracted the ___-coordinates.

skills.name: Solve a real-world problem by combining distances on a coordinate map

prerequisite_skill.description: Find single horizontal or vertical distances between points and add them, applying any unit scale stated in the problem.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: On a map where one unit equals 10 meters, how many meters is it from (1, 2) to (1, 5)?

skills.i_do_script: Real-world coordinate problems usually involve more than one segment. I find each segment's distance one at a time, then I combine them — sometimes by adding (total trip), sometimes by subtracting (how much farther). Watch: refrigerator at (6, 4), couch at (-2, 4), bed at (-2, -5). Couch-to-fridge: y matches, so |6 - (-2)| = 8. Couch-to-bed: x matches, so |4 - (-5)| = 9. Difference = 9 - 8 = 1. The bed is 1 unit farther from the couch than the fridge is.

canonical_error.pattern: Computes each distance correctly but then mis-combines them — adds when the question asks for a difference, or applies the unit scale only once instead of to every segment.
canonical_error.example: Asked which distance is greater and by how much, the student adds 9 + 8 = 17 instead of subtracting; or, on a map where each unit equals 10 meters, they answer '1 unit' instead of '10 meters.'
canonical_error.why: The student treats the problem as a one-step distance question and answers as soon as they find a number, without rereading what the problem actually asked or applying the stated scale to the final answer.

redirect_script.stop: Pause — what is the question really asking?
redirect_script.prompt: Reread the last sentence and underline the verb (total, difference, farther). Then check whether each unit equals 1 or something bigger.
redirect_script.praise: Good — you found the distances AND answered the actual question. Strong finish.

vocabulary.definition: A flat surface with an x-axis and a y-axis used to locate points.
One step of length on the grid. The problem may say each unit equals a different real-world length, like 1 block or 10 meters.

practice_problems.stem: On a map, each grid unit represents 10 meters. Two points are 4 units apart on the grid. How many meters apart are they really?
practice_problems.answer: 40 meters

practice_problems.stem: A library is at (2, 5) and a school is at (2, 1). How many units apart are they?
practice_problems.answer: 4 units

practice_problems.stem: A home is at (-3, 2), a park is at (4, 2), and a fountain is at (4, 6). Each unit is 1 block. How many blocks is the walk from home to the park, then from the park to the fountain?
practice_problems.answer: 11 blocks. Home to park: |4 - (-3)| = 7. Park to fountain: |6 - 2| = 4. Total: 7 + 4 = 11.

practice_problems.stem: A couch is at (-5, 3), a TV is at (7, 3), and a lamp is at (-5, -6). Which is farther from the couch -- the TV or the lamp -- and by how much?
practice_problems.answer: The TV. Couch to TV: |7 - (-5)| = 12. Couch to lamp: |3 - (-6)| = 9. The TV is 3 units farther.
practice_problems.notes: The question asks for a comparison -- adding 12 + 9 = 21 is the classic wrong move.

practice_problems.stem: A student solved this map problem. Find the mistake and fix it.
shown_work: A map uses a scale of 1 unit = 5 meters.
A bench is at (1, -2) and a fountain is at (1, 4).
The fountain is 6 meters from the bench.
practice_problems.answer: The grid distance of 6 units is right, but each unit stands for 5 meters. The real distance is 6 x 5 = 30 meters.
practice_problems.notes: Baits the canonical error's scale piece: the last step of the problem never happened.

practice_problems.stem: The map shows a school S, a store T, and a gym G. Each unit is 1 block. How many blocks is the walk from S to T to G?
Ravi starts at (-2, -1), walks 6 blocks east, then 3 blocks north. What are the coordinates where he ends, and how long was his whole walk?
practice_problems.answer: He ends at (4, 2), and the walk is 6 + 3 = 9 blocks.
practice_problems.notes: Reverses the direction: moves are given, coordinates are produced.

practice_problems.stem: Make your own map: place three locations A, B, and C so that the L-shaped path A to B to C is exactly 10 units long (A and B share a y-coordinate; B and C share an x-coordinate). Give the coordinates.
practice_problems.notes: Producing a path shows the distance rule runs both directions.

activities.title: Design a Neighborhood Map
activities.instructions:
1. Each student plots four locations (home, school, store, park) at grid points, keeping at least two pairs on a shared grid line.
2. Each student writes two distance questions about their own map -- one 'total trip' question and one 'how much farther' question -- and solves them on the back.
3. Partners swap maps and answer each other's questions, remembering the scale card: every answer must be in blocks, not units.
4. Swap back and check.
5. Debrief question: where did the scale sneak into (or out of) your answers?

activities.title: The Missing Scale
materials: One printed problem card per group
activities.instructions:
1. Show the group the student work and let them find the problem before you speak.
2. Ask: what did this student do RIGHT? (The absolute value work is perfect.)
3. Ask: what does '1 unit = 5 meters' mean for the final answer?
4. Each student writes the corrected final line and a one-sentence tip about reading the scale.
5. Debrief question: at what point in a map problem should you look for the scale?

content.worked_problem: Map scale: 1 unit = 5 meters. Bench at (1, -2), fountain at (1, 4). Student's work: |4 - (-2)| = 6, so the fountain is 6 meters away.
content.error_step: The student stopped at the grid distance and never applied the scale.
content.why: 6 counts units on the grid. Each unit stands for 5 real meters, so the real distance is 6 x 5 = 30 meters.

strategy_links.why: Pairs restating 'what is this question actually asking' catches the add-versus-compare trap before any math starts.
Thinking aloud through a multi-part map problem models the reread-the-question habit this skill's canonical error lacks.
Multi-step route problems layer well: model one leg, share one leg, release the combining step to the student.

questioning_prompts: What does the question ask for -- a total, a difference, or a comparison? Underline the words that say so.
How many separate straight-line legs are in this trip?
What does one grid unit stand for in THIS problem?
On this leg of the trip, which coordinate stays the same?
You have two distances. What does the question want you to DO with them?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student finds both distances correctly, then adds them when the question asks how much farther -- or leaves the answer in grid units when a scale was given.
misconception_redirects.say: Reread the last sentence and underline the verb (total, difference, farther). Then check whether each unit equals 1 or something bigger.
misconception_redirects.praise: Good -- you found the distances AND answered the actual question. Strong finish.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student tries to find a distance between two points that share NEITHER coordinate, drawing a diagonal.
misconception_redirects.say: In this unit we only measure straight across or straight up-and-down. Find the corner point that shares one coordinate with each end, and break the trip into two straight legs.
misconception_redirects.praise: Nice -- you split the diagonal trip into two grid-line legs.

quick_checks.prompt: A couch is at (-2, 4) and a bed is at (-2, -5). How far apart?
quick_checks.look_for: 9 units, via |4 - (-5)|. An answer of 1 means the signs got dropped; 0 means the matching x-coordinates were subtracted.

quick_checks.prompt: Each unit is 10 meters and the grid distance is 7 units. Real distance?
quick_checks.look_for: 70 meters. Answering '7' means the scale never got applied -- the canonical last-step miss.

worked_example_script.text: Post the problem: a refrigerator is at (6, 4), a couch at (-2, 4), and a bed at (-2, -5). How much farther from the couch is the bed than the refrigerator?
Before any math -- what is this question actually asking for? A total distance, or a comparison?
Couch to refrigerator: which coordinate matches? Set up the distance with absolute value bars.
Couch to bed: which coordinate matches this time? Set that one up too.
Write the two results side by side: refrigerator 8 units, bed 9 units.
If the student adds 8 + 9 = 17, point back at the question: 'Does how much farther mean combine the trips, or compare them?' Have them underline 'farther.'
So how much farther is the bed? And if each unit were 10 meters, what would you do to that answer?
Find each straight-line distance first, then reread the question to decide how to combine them -- and always apply the scale last.

worked_solution.stem: A refrigerator is at (6, 4), a couch at (-2, 4), and a bed at (-2, -5). How much farther from the couch is the bed than the refrigerator?
worked_solution.answer: The bed is 1 unit farther from the couch than the refrigerator.

steps.annotation: Same y-coordinate means a horizontal leg -- subtract the x-values inside bars.
Same x-coordinate means a vertical leg -- subtract the y-values inside bars.
'How much farther' asks for a difference, so subtract the two distances -- don't add them.

faded_example.stem: A school is at (-3, -2), a park at (5, -2), and a pool at (5, 3). Each unit is 1 block. How many blocks is the walk from the school to the park to the pool?

steps.math: School to park: y matches -> |5 - (-3)| = 8 blocks.
steps.annotation: The first leg is done for you.
Park to pool: which coordinate matches? Find that leg's length.
The question asks for the whole walk. Combine the legs.

sentence_starters: The question asks for ___, so after finding each distance I ___.
Each grid unit stands for ___, so my final answer is ___.

skills.name: Find every point a given distance from a starting point along an axis

prerequisite_skill.description: Reverse the distance procedure — given a starting point and a target distance, generate the coordinates that are exactly that far away horizontally or vertically.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Starting at (-8, 9), name two points that are exactly 14 units away with the same y-coordinate.

skills.i_do_script: To find every point a given distance from a starting point along an axis, I work backwards from the distance rule. If the points must share a y-coordinate, the distance comes from changing x, so I add and subtract the distance from the starting x. Same logic for shared x. Watch: from (-8, 9) at 14 units along the same horizontal line, x = -8 + 14 = 6 or x = -8 - 14 = -22, so (6, 9) and (-22, 9). Vertically, y = 9 + 14 = 23 or 9 - 14 = -5, so (-8, 23) and (-8, -5). Four valid points total.

canonical_error.pattern: Finds only one direction (only adds, or only subtracts) instead of giving both the +d and -d points, missing half the valid answers.
canonical_error.example: Asked for points 14 units from (-8, 9), the student lists only (6, 9) and (-8, 23) — they added in both directions but never subtracted, missing (-22, 9) and (-8, -5).
canonical_error.why: The student treats 'distance' as one-directional motion (forward or up). They have not internalized that a fixed distance from a point produces TWO solutions on each axis (one in each direction), giving four total when both axes are considered.

redirect_script.stop: Hold on — distance goes both ways.
redirect_script.prompt: For each axis, write two equations: one with + the distance and one with - the distance. Then check which valid points the answer choices match.
redirect_script.praise: Excellent — you found all four. Distance always goes both ways.

vocabulary.definition: Distance from zero. Because |d| and |-d| are the same, a distance produces two locations on each axis.
The grid formed by the x-axis and y-axis where points are plotted.

next_steps.if_pass: Ready for 7.AF.5 (work with rational coordinates and slope).

practice_problems.stem: Start at (2, 3) and move 4 units up. What point are you on?
What two numbers on a number line are exactly 6 units from 0?
practice_problems.answer: 6 and -6

practice_problems.stem: Name BOTH points that are exactly 5 units from (3, -1) and have the same x-coordinate as it.
practice_problems.notes: -1 + 5 = 4 and -1 - 5 = -6. One answer only means the both-directions idea hasn't landed.

practice_problems.stem: Name ALL FOUR points that are exactly 7 units from (-2, 5) and share an x- or y-coordinate with it.
A student listed every point 6 units from (4, -3) along a grid line. Find the mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Find every point 6 units from (4, -3) on the same vertical or horizontal line.
practice_problems.answer: Both points are correct, but distance goes BOTH ways -- the student only added. Subtracting gives (4, -9) and (-2, -3). Four points in all.
practice_problems.notes: Baits the canonical one-direction error with fresh numbers.

practice_problems.stem: A carrot patch is at (-8, 9) on a garden map. Tomatoes are planted exactly 14 feet away along a grid line (each unit is 1 foot). Which of these is NOT a possible tomato location?
practice_problems.notes: (-6, 9) is only |(-6) - (-8)| = 2 feet away. The other three are all exactly 14.

practice_problems.stem: A sprinkler at (1.5, -2) sprays exactly 3.5 feet along the grid lines. Name the four points at the edge of its spray.
practice_problems.notes: Decimals per the spec's difficult tier: 1.5 +/- 3.5 and -2 +/- 3.5.

practice_problems.stem: How many points are exactly 4 units from (0, 0) and share a coordinate with it? Explain why the answer is more than two.
practice_problems.answer: Four: (4, 0), (-4, 0), (0, 4), and (0, -4). Each grid direction gives two points, because a distance can be measured in the + direction or the - direction.
practice_problems.notes: Explain-why stretch -- the reason, not just the list.

activities.title: Plus-Sign Plot
activities.instructions:
1. Each student draws a center-and-distance card and plots the center point.
2. Plot every point that is exactly that distance away along a grid line -- students should discover there are four.
3. Connect each outer point to the center: the picture forms a plus sign.
4. Label each arm with its expression, like -1 + 4 = 3.
5. Debrief question: why does every card make a plus sign with four tips -- never three, never one?

activities.title: Treasure Radius
materials: One four-quadrant grid per pair (-12 to 12)
activities.instructions:
1. Partner A announces a landmark point and a distance, like 'the well is at (-3, 4), the treasure is exactly 6 units away along a grid line.'
2. Partner A secretly marks the treasure at one of the valid spots.
3. Partner B lists EVERY possible treasure spot first (there should be four), then gets two guesses.
4. If B's list is missing a spot, A scores a point; if B guesses the treasure, B scores two.
5. Swap roles. Debrief question: how did you make sure your list was complete?

strategy_links.why: 'How many answers should exist?' is a perfect pair-discussion prompt before anyone starts computing.
A complete four-point worked example next to a two-point flawed one makes the missing-directions bug visible.
Whiteboard Pass shows instantly which students stopped at one or two points instead of four.

questioning_prompts: You found one point -- is it the ONLY one? How could you convince me?
If the new point shares an x-coordinate with the start, which coordinate is allowed to change?
What does absolute value tell you about the + direction and the - direction?
How many points should you expect in total? Why four?
Check one of your points: is it really that exact distance away? Prove it with an expression.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student finds only the added points (one per axis) and stops, missing the subtracted ones.
misconception_redirects.say: For each axis, write two equations: one with + the distance and one with - the distance. Then check which valid points the answer choices match.
misconception_redirects.praise: Excellent -- you found all four. Distance always goes both ways.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student changes BOTH coordinates at once, like (4 + 6, -3 + 6), drifting diagonally off the grid line.
misconception_redirects.say: Along a grid line only ONE coordinate may change. Freeze one coordinate with your finger and move the other by the distance.
misconception_redirects.praise: Yes -- one coordinate frozen, the other moved. That keeps you on the grid line.

quick_checks.prompt: Name the points 3 units from (5, 5) with the same y-coordinate.
quick_checks.look_for: (8, 5) and (2, 5) -- both. One answer means the both-directions idea hasn't landed yet.

quick_checks.prompt: From (0, -4), go 6 units along the same vertical line. Name both points.
quick_checks.look_for: (0, 2) and (0, -10). A slip like (0, -2) shows the count across zero broke down.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: 'Name every point exactly 14 units from (-8, 9) that shares a coordinate with it.'
Suppose the new point shares the y-coordinate 9. Which coordinate is allowed to change?
Move the x-coordinate 14 units in the positive direction. What is -8 + 14, and what point does that give?
Most students stop after adding. Ask: 'Is (6, 9) the only point on that horizontal line that's 14 away? What about the other direction?'
Now subtract: what is -8 - 14? Careful with the signs -- count it out if you need to.
We have both horizontal points. Now freeze x at -8 and move along the vertical line. What two points do you get?
Check the subtraction 9 - 14 -- students often say -6 or 5. Have them count down through zero: 9 down to 0 is 9 units, then 5 more is -5.
A fixed distance along grid lines always gives four points: two horizontal, two vertical. If you found fewer, a direction is missing.

worked_solution.stem: Name every point exactly 14 units from (-8, 9) that shares a coordinate with it.

steps.annotation: Freeze the y-coordinate at 9 and add the distance to x.
Distance goes both ways -- subtract the distance too.
Repeat both directions on the y-coordinate, with x frozen at -8.
A fixed distance along grid lines always gives two points per axis -- four in all.

faded_example.stem: Name every point exactly 5 units from (3, -2) that shares a coordinate with it.

steps.annotation: The first direction is done for you.
Distance goes both ways: subtract 5 from the x-coordinate. What point do you get?
Now freeze x at 3 and move the y-coordinate both directions. Name both points.

sentence_starters: Distance goes both ways, so I wrote ___ + ___ AND ___ - ___.
I expect ___ points in total because each grid direction gives ___.

skills.name: Plot a point in the first quadrant from a whole-number ordered pair

prerequisite_skill.description: Identify the x-axis and y-axis on a coordinate grid; know that the origin is (0, 0).
prerequisite_skill.check_question: On a coordinate grid, where is the point (0, 0)?

skills.i_do_script: Watch me plot the point (4, 3). Step 1: I always start at the origin — that's the dot where the x-axis and y-axis cross, labeled O at (0, 0). Step 2: The first number in the pair is the x-coordinate, so it tells me how far to move RIGHT along the x-axis. The first number is 4, so I count one, two, three, four units to the right and stop on the x-axis. Step 3: The second number is the y-coordinate, so it tells me how far to move UP from where I just stopped. The second number is 3, so from (4, 0) I count one, two, three units up. Step 4: I draw a dot right there. That dot is (4, 3). Notice the order: x first (right), y second (up) — like reading 'right then up.' Both numbers are positive, so I never move left or down — I stay in the top-right region, which is Quadrant I.

canonical_error.pattern: Counts the y-coordinate up from the origin instead of up from the point already reached on the x-axis, OR moves diagonally instead of taking two separate axis-aligned steps.
canonical_error.example: Asked to plot (4, 3), the student moves right 4 to land at (4, 0), then forgets to go up and circles (4, 0); or the student moves diagonally up-right four-and-then-three steps and lands somewhere like (3, 4) or (5, 2) because they did not separate the two motions.
canonical_error.why: The student knows 'right and up' but treats the two moves as a single fuzzy gesture rather than two distinct, axis-aligned steps that compose. Without the explicit pause at (x, 0) before moving up, the student loses track of which number controls which direction.

redirect_script.stop: Wait — let me see the path from the origin.
redirect_script.prompt: Start at (0, 0). Move along the x-axis the number of units the first coordinate says (right for positive). Then turn and move up the number of units the second coordinate says. No diagonals — two separate moves.
redirect_script.praise: You moved right first, then up — that's exactly the order ordered pairs work.

next_steps.if_pass: Move on to 6AF5-S1: read the coordinates of an already-plotted point in any quadrant.
next_steps.if_fail: Reteach with 6AF5-F1 (ordered pair convention) before retrying plotting.

sample_items.stem: Where would you plot the point (4, 3)?
sample_items.answer: Start at (0,0). Move 4 units right along the x-axis to (4,0), then move 3 units up to land at (4,3).
sample_items.distractor_logic: A student who moves diagonally lands at the wrong spot; a student who counts y from the origin instead of from (4,0) ends up off the intended location.

sample_items.stem: Where would you plot the point (2, 7)?
sample_items.answer: Start at (0,0). Move 2 units right along the x-axis to (2,0), then move 7 units up to land at (2,7).
sample_items.distractor_logic: Reversing the coordinates would land at (7,2); moving diagonally would skip the axis-aligned steps.

sample_items.stem: Where would you plot the point (6, 1)?
sample_items.answer: Start at (0,0). Move 6 units right along the x-axis to (6,0), then move 1 unit up to land at (6,1).
sample_items.distractor_logic: A student who counts up first then right would land at (1,6); moving diagonally loses track of which step is which.

sample_items.stem: Plot the point (5, 2). Which of these describes the correct location?
sample_items.answer: Move 5 units right from the origin to (5,0), then 2 units up to (5,2).
choices: Move 5 units right from the origin to (5,0), then 2 units up to (5,2).
Move 2 units right from the origin to (2,0), then 5 units up to (2,5).
Move diagonally up and to the right until you have taken 5 steps right and 2 steps up at the same time.
Move 5 units up from the origin to (0,5), then 2 units right to (2,5).
sample_items.distractor_logic: Choice 2 reverses x and y; Choice 3 is diagonal motion; Choice 4 counts y from the origin first instead of from (x,0).

sample_items.stem: Where would you plot the point (8, 4)?
sample_items.answer: Start at (0,0). Move 8 units right along the x-axis to (8,0), then move 4 units up to land at (8,4).
sample_items.distractor_logic: Reversing coordinates lands at (4,8); diagonal motion blurs the two steps into one.

sample_items.stem: Where would you plot the point (3, 9)?
sample_items.answer: Start at (0,0). Move 3 units right along the x-axis to (3,0), then move 9 units up to land at (3,9).
sample_items.distractor_logic: Counting y up from origin first lands at (0,9) before going right, producing (9,9) or other errors; reversing gives (9,3).

sample_items.stem: Plot the point (7, 6). Which of these describes the correct location?
sample_items.answer: Move 7 units right along the x-axis to (7,0), then 6 units up to (7,6).
choices: Move 6 units right along the x-axis to (6,0), then 7 units up to (6,7).
Move 7 units right along the x-axis to (7,0), then 6 units up to (7,6).
Move 7 units up the y-axis to (0,7), then 6 units right to (6,7).
Move diagonally so each step goes one right and one up until you reach (7,6).
sample_items.distractor_logic: Choice 1 reverses x and y; Choice 3 counts y from origin instead of from (x,0); Choice 4 collapses the two motions into a diagonal.

sample_items.stem: Where would you plot the point (1, 5)?
sample_items.answer: Start at (0,0). Move 1 unit right along the x-axis to (1,0), then move 5 units up to land at (1,5).
sample_items.distractor_logic: Reversing the order lands at (5,1); skipping the pause at (1,0) leads to imprecise diagonal motion.

sample_items.stem: Where would you plot the point (9, 2)?
sample_items.answer: Start at (0,0). Move 9 units right along the x-axis to (9,0), then move 2 units up to land at (9,2).
sample_items.distractor_logic: Diagonal motion makes the student arrive at a fuzzy spot near (9,2) but not exactly there; reversing gives (2,9).

sample_items.stem: Where would you plot the point (0, 6)?
sample_items.answer: Start at (0,0). Move 0 units right (stay on the y-axis), then move 6 units up to land at (0,6).
sample_items.distractor_logic: A student who treats x=0 as 'no rule' may move diagonally; reversing gives (6,0) which is on the x-axis instead.

sample_items.stem: Plot the point (4, 0). Which of these describes the correct location?
sample_items.answer: Move 4 units right along the x-axis to (4,0), then move 0 units up — stay on the x-axis.
choices: Move 0 units right, then 4 units up to (0,4).
Move 4 units up the y-axis to (0,4), then stop.
Move 4 units right along the x-axis to (4,0), then move 0 units up — stay on the x-axis.
Move diagonally 4 units up and to the right.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Choice 1 reverses coordinates; Choice 2 mistakes x for y and counts up the y-axis; Choice 4 substitutes diagonal motion for axis-aligned steps.

sample_items.stem: Where would you plot the point (5, 5)?
sample_items.answer: Start at (0,0). Move 5 units right along the x-axis to (5,0), then move 5 units up to land at (5,5).
sample_items.distractor_logic: When x and y are equal, students may shortcut by moving diagonally five steps and lose precision; the correct path is two distinct axis-aligned steps.

sample_items.stem: Where would you plot the point (10, 3)?
sample_items.answer: Start at (0,0). Move 10 units right along the x-axis to (10,0), then move 3 units up to land at (10,3).
sample_items.distractor_logic: Reversing the order lands at (3,10); counting up from origin first lands at (0,3) and then 10 right gives the same point only by accident in this case, but the procedure is wrong.

sample_items.stem: Where would you plot the point (2, 10)?
sample_items.answer: Start at (0,0). Move 2 units right along the x-axis to (2,0), then move 10 units up to land at (2,10).
sample_items.distractor_logic: Reversing gives (10,2); diagonal motion across a long y-gap compounds error quickly.

sample_items.stem: Plot the point (3, 8). Which of these describes the correct location?
sample_items.answer: Move 3 units right along the x-axis to (3,0), then 8 units up to (3,8).
choices: Move 8 units right along the x-axis to (8,0), then 3 units up to (8,3).
Move 3 units up the y-axis to (0,3), then 8 units right to (8,3).
Move 3 units right along the x-axis to (3,0), then 8 units up to (3,8).
Move diagonally up and to the right until you have moved a total of 3 across and 8 up in one combined motion.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Choice 1 reverses x and y; Choice 2 counts y up from the origin first instead of from (x,0); Choice 4 replaces two axis-aligned steps with one diagonal motion.

sample_items.stem: Where would you plot the point (7, 0)?
sample_items.answer: Start at (0,0). Move 7 units right along the x-axis to (7,0), then move 0 units up — the point sits on the x-axis at (7,0).
sample_items.distractor_logic: A student who reverses gives (0,7) which is on the y-axis; one who insists on a 'second motion' may add an unintended up-step.

sample_items.stem: Where would you plot the point (6, 4)?
sample_items.answer: Start at (0,0). Move 6 units right along the x-axis to (6,0), then move 4 units up to land at (6,4).
sample_items.distractor_logic: Reversing lands at (4,6); diagonal motion lands somewhere along the line from origin to (6,4) but not necessarily at the lattice point.

sample_items.stem: Plot the point (1, 1). Which of these describes the correct location?
sample_items.answer: Move 1 unit right along the x-axis to (1,0), then 1 unit up to (1,1).
choices: Move diagonally one step up and to the right from the origin.
Move 1 unit right along the x-axis to (1,0), then 1 unit up to (1,1).
Move 1 unit up the y-axis to (0,1), then stop.
Move 2 units total in a single up-right motion from the origin.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Choice 1 substitutes a diagonal step for two axis-aligned steps; Choice 3 counts y from origin and forgets the x-step; Choice 4 conflates the two coordinates into one combined motion.

sample_items.stem: Where would you plot the point (9, 9)?
sample_items.answer: Start at (0,0). Move 9 units right along the x-axis to (9,0), then move 9 units up to land at (9,9).
sample_items.distractor_logic: Equal coordinates tempt diagonal motion; without the explicit pause at (9,0) the student cannot guarantee landing on the lattice point.

sample_items.stem: Plot the point (8, 2). Which of these describes the correct location?
sample_items.answer: Move 8 units right along the x-axis to (8,0), then 2 units up to (8,2).
choices: Move 2 units right along the x-axis to (2,0), then 8 units up to (2,8).
Move 8 units up the y-axis to (0,8), then 2 units right to (2,8).
Move diagonally up and to the right until you have moved 8 right and 2 up in one combined motion.
Move 8 units right along the x-axis to (8,0), then 2 units up to (8,2).
sample_items.distractor_logic: Choice 1 reverses x and y; Choice 2 counts y from origin first instead of from (x,0); Choice 3 collapses the two axis-aligned steps into a diagonal.

practice_problems.stem: Start at the origin and move 3 units right along the x-axis. What point are you standing on?
In the ordered pair (5, 2), which number tells you how far to move right?
practice_problems.answer: The first number, 5 -- the x-coordinate.

practice_problems.stem: Plot the point (2, 6). Describe your two moves from the origin.
practice_problems.answer: Move right 2 to (2, 0), then up 6 to (2, 6).
practice_problems.notes: Listen for the pause at (2, 0) -- the second count must start there, not at the origin.

practice_problems.stem: Plot (7, 3) and (3, 7) on the same grid. Are they the same point? How do you know?
practice_problems.answer: No. (7, 3) is right 7 then up 3; (3, 7) is right 3 then up 7 -- two different spots.

practice_problems.stem: A student plotted the point (4, 6). Find the mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: The first number is the x-coordinate -- it moves you RIGHT, not up. Correct path: right 4 to (4, 0), then up 6. The dot belongs at (4, 6).
practice_problems.notes: Baits the canonical error: matching the first number to the vertical axis.

practice_problems.stem: A point sits 5 units right of the origin and 0 units up. Name its ordered pair.
practice_problems.notes: Zero coordinates trip students who think every point needs two moves.

practice_problems.stem: Write the ordered pair for the point you reach by moving 9 units up from (2, 0).
A dot is drawn at (6, 2). Write walking directions from the origin to the dot using only the words right and up.
practice_problems.answer: Move right 6 units, then up 2 units.
practice_problems.notes: Producing the directions reverses the skill -- reading the plot back into moves.

activities.title: Walk the Grid
materials: Painter's tape floor grid (or a large paper grid)
activities.instructions:
1. Mark the origin on the floor grid and label the x-axis and y-axis with tape.
2. One student draws an ordered-pair card, like (4, 3), and reads it aloud.
3. Another student stands on the origin and walks it: right first, then up -- pausing and saying the stop point, like '(4, 0).'
4. The group checks: two straight walks, no diagonals.
5. Debrief question: why do we always pause on the x-axis before turning?

activities.title: First-Quadrant Battleship
activities.instructions:
1. Each partner secretly marks 4 single-point 'ships' at grid intersections on their own grid.
2. Partners take turns calling ordered pairs, like (6, 2). The caller must say the pair; the opponent answers hit or miss.
3. Both players record every call on their grids -- callers mark misses too, so wrong plots cost turns.
4. First to find all 4 ships wins.
5. Debrief question: what happened when someone mixed up the two numbers in a pair?

strategy_links.why: Walking the grid physically (concrete) before pencil plotting (abstract) anchors the right-then-up convention in the body.
Narrating 'right 4... pause at (4, 0)... up 3' aloud makes the two separate moves visible before they blur into a diagonal.
Whiteboard Pass shows every student's plotted point at once, so a reversed pair is caught on the spot.

questioning_prompts: Which number in the pair moves you along the x-axis?
Where do you pause before you start moving up?
What would happen if you did the two moves in the other order -- same point or different?
Trace the path with your finger. Did you make two straight moves or one diagonal one?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student counts the y-coordinate up from the origin instead of from the stop point on the x-axis, or slides diagonally toward the point.
misconception_redirects.say: Start at (0, 0). Move along the x-axis the number of units the first coordinate says (right for positive). Then turn and move up the number of units the second coordinate says. No diagonals -- two separate moves.
misconception_redirects.praise: You moved right first, then up -- that's exactly the order ordered pairs work.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student swaps the coordinates -- plots (3, 5) at the spot for (5, 3).
misconception_redirects.say: Point at the first number and say 'x -- right.' Point at the second and say 'y -- up.' Now walk the path again with those labels out loud.
misconception_redirects.praise: X first, y second -- you matched each number to its axis.

quick_checks.prompt: Plot (6, 1) while I watch your pencil.
quick_checks.look_for: Two separate moves with a pause at (6, 0). A diagonal slide or a dot at (1, 6) means the convention isn't set yet.
On the y-axis, 4 up. Answering (4, 0)'s spot means the number got matched to the wrong axis.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a first-quadrant grid on the board and write the ordered pair (4, 3) next to it.
Every plot starts at the same spot. Where is it? Put your finger there.
The first number is 4. Which direction does the first number move you -- and along which axis?
If the student moves up 4, stop before the dot goes down. Ask: 'Which number is the x-coordinate, and which axis is the x-axis?'
Trace right 4 along the x-axis and draw a small pause mark at (4, 0).
We paused at (4, 0). What does the 3 tell you to do now -- and where do you count from?
Watch for counting the 3 up from the origin instead of from (4, 0). If it happens, have the student put a finger on (4, 0) and count up out loud from there.
Right 4, pause, up 3 -- two separate moves, never a diagonal. The dot at (4, 3) is the point.

worked_solution.stem: Plot the point (4, 3). Describe every move.
worked_solution.answer: Right 4 to (4, 0), then up 3 -- the dot goes at (4, 3).

steps.annotation: Every plot starts where the two axes cross.
The first number is the x-coordinate. It always moves you left or right.
Count up from where you stopped -- not from the origin.
Two separate straight moves, right then up -- never one diagonal slide.

faded_example.stem: Plot the point (5, 2). Describe every move.
faded_example.answer: Right 5 to (5, 0), then up 2 -- the dot goes at (5, 2).

steps.annotation: The starting spot is given.
Which way does the 5 move you, and what point do you pause on?
Which way does the 2 move you? Name the final point.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S3, solving a real-world map problem by combining absolute-value distances, the At-proficiency core. If they pass, move up to S4, generating every point a given distance away along a grid line. If they fail, drop one grade: B1 checks first-quadrant plotting and B2 checks generating ordered pairs from two rules, the grade 5 skills this standard's graphing leans on. If those wobble, the foundations F1 (number-line location and distance) and F2 (extending patterns by a rule) locate the gap in grades 3 and 4. S5, S1, and S2 remain available to probe the standard's own plotting, quadrant, and single-distance groundwork.
